Recursion is a programming concept where a function solves a problem by calling itself to handle smaller, more manageable pieces of the task. Think of it like Russian nesting dolls: to find the smallest doll, you keep opening the current doll to reveal the next one inside. Every recursive function needs a "base case," which is the condition that tells it to stop calling itself and prevents an infinite loop. Once the base case is reached, the results are passed back up the chain until the original problem is fully solved.
